metadata.title: 2009 Case 23
metadata.original_presentation: A 13-year-old boy was admitted to the hospital because of headache, nausea, seizures, renal failure, and hypertension.

required.content: What is the patient's recent medical history?
required.response: The patient had been well until approximately 3 weeks earlier, when intermittent left-sided headaches and fatigue developed, followed by nasal congestion and anorexia. He began to nap daily after school. During the week before admission, nausea and vomiting occurred approximately every other day. Five days before admission, facial and periorbital swelling developed.

teaching_points.content: Headaches, fatigue, and facial swelling can be indicative of underlying systemic issues such as renal or cardiovascular problems.

required.content: What were the patient's symptoms on the day of admission?
required.response: On the morning of admission, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain developed while the patient was at school. He reported numbness of the right leg and dizziness, and he became disoriented, with difficulty walking and coordinating his legs.

teaching_points.content: Acute neurological symptoms such as numbness and disorientation can suggest a vascular or metabolic cause.

required.content: What is the patient's past medical history?
required.response: He had been born via vaginal delivery after a full-term gestation. At 3 weeks of age, he required surgery for pyloric stenosis. One year before admission, on routine examination, the blood pressure was 100/70 mm Hg and pubertal development had begun.

teaching_points.content: Past surgical history and developmental milestones can provide context for current health status.

required.content: What is the family medical history?
required.response: Both grandfathers had had prostate cancer, and there was a family history of migraine headaches. There was no family history of an autoimmune disorder.

teaching_points.content: Family history can help identify genetic predispositions to certain conditions.

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Acute Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis
refuting_evidence: no specific evidence refuting this diagnosis

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Hypertensive Encephalopathy
refuting_evidence: no specific evidence refuting this diagnosis

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)
refuting_evidence: no family history of autoimmune disorder

required.content: What were the findings on physical examination in the emergency department?
required.response: The patient was awake, oriented, and vomiting intermittently. The blood pressure was 170/120 mm Hg, the pulse 63 beats per minute, the temperature 37°C, the respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, the oxygen saturation 98% while he was breathing ambient air, and the weight 45.5 kg. The skin was pale and facial edema was present; the remainder of the examination was normal.

teaching_points.content: Hypertension in children can be a sign of renal or endocrine disorders.

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Hypertensive Encephalopathy
refuting_evidence: no focal neurological deficits noted on examination

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Pheochromocytoma
refuting_evidence: no family history of endocrine disorders

required.content: What were the results of the initial laboratory tests?
required.response: Laboratory-test results revealed azotemia. Screening tests for mononucleosis and hepatitis A, B, and C were negative.

teaching_points.content: Azotemia indicates impaired kidney function and requires further investigation.

required.content: What did the CT scan of the head show?
required.response: CT of the head showed a small, ill-defined focus of decreased density in the right parietal region and no other evidence of focal or diffuse lesions, hemorrhage, hydrocephalus, or focal bone lesions.

teaching_points.content: CT findings can help rule out acute intracranial events such as hemorrhage or stroke.

required.content: What were the findings from the MRI of the brain?
required.response: MRI of the brain showed areas of increased T2-weighted signal intensity in the subcortical white matter in the frontal, parietal, and occipital regions, with a predominantly normal signal on diffusion-weighted imaging.

teaching_points.content: MRI can provide detailed information about brain tissue changes that are not visible on CT.

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Hypertensive Encephalopathy
supporting_evidence: MRI findings of increased T2-weighted signal intensity in subcortical white matter

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Acute Glomerulonephritis
refuting_evidence: No mention of hematuria or proteinuria

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES)
supporting_evidence: MRI findings of increased T2-weighted signal intensity in subcortical white matter
refuting_evidence: No specific mention of visual disturbances
additional_information_needed: Follow-up MRI after blood pressure control

current_ideal_differential_diagnosis.name: Vasculitis (e.g., Polyarteritis Nodosa)
refuting_evidence: No family history of autoimmune disorder
additional_information_needed: ANCA, ANA, and other autoimmune panels
Biopsy of affected tissue if indicated

required.content: What treatments were administered to the patient?
required.response: Labetalol and ondansetron were administered, and the blood pressure decreased to 132/83 mm Hg. A continuous intravenous infusion of nitroprusside was begun, with a goal of systolic pressures below 140 mm Hg. Labetalol and ondansetron were continued, and hydralazine, calcium gluconate, insulin, and dextrose were given intravenously. Emergency hemodialysis was performed. Fluid was restricted to 1 liter per day, and methylprednisolone and ranitidine were begun. Mannitol, midazolam, and fentanyl citrate were added. Magnesium was administered as needed.

teaching_points.content: Management of hypertensive emergencies in children involves careful blood pressure control and addressing underlying causes.
